= tests/thirdparty - functional tests for the shipped third-party libraries
:toc: macro
:toclevels: 2

Tests the libraries that the toolchain sysroot ships, *directly*: through their
own public headers and ABI, with no stappler/xenolith module in the link. Only
`runtime` is linked, because that is what the libraries themselves were built
against (glibc on Linux, the freestanding libc on Windows).

That isolation is the point. When `stappler_network` or `stappler_crypto`
misbehaves on a target, this suite answers the first question -- *is the shipped
library itself healthy on this target?* -- without engine code in the way.

toc::[]

== Running

[source,sh]
----
tests/thirdparty/run.sh                 # build + run host and Windows (wine)
tests/thirdparty/run.sh --host-only
tests/thirdparty/run.sh --win-only
tests/thirdparty/run.sh --network       # also hit the public internet
tests/thirdparty/run.sh -v openssl_ec   # one test, full output
----

Or drive the binary directly:

[source,sh]
----
make -C tests/thirdparty STAPPLER_TARGET=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -j8
tests/thirdparty/stappler-build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/cc/thirdpartytest --list
tests/thirdparty/stappler-build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/cc/thirdpartytest openssl_digest
----

Every check prints one `[ OK ]` / `[FAIL]` line; the exit status is the number of
failed checks. A test named on the command line always runs, whatever its flags
say -- naming it *is* the opt-in.

[cols="1,4"]
|===
| `--network` | run the tests that need a route to the public internet (`curl_https`)
| `--no-sockets` | skip the tests that need loopback TCP (`curl_tls_loopback`)
| `--list` | print the test names, one per line
|===

== What is covered

=== OpenSSL (`lib/openssl.cpp`)

Where a published test vector exists it is checked byte for byte, so a
miscompiled or misconfigured build shows up as a *wrong value*, not as a missing
symbol.

[cols="1,3"]
|===
| `openssl_version` | linked libcrypto matches the headers; the default provider is available
| `openssl_digest` | MD5 / SHA-1 / SHA-2 / SHA-3 over `"abc"`; empty input; chunked == one-shot; `EVP_MD_fetch`
| `openssl_hmac` | RFC 4231 cases 1-2 (SHA-256/512), RFC 2202 case 2 (SHA-1), the same via `EVP_MAC`
| `openssl_cipher` | AES-128-ECB (FIPS-197 C.1), AES-128-GCM (spec case 3, ciphertext *and* tag, plus tag rejection), AES-256-CBC round trip, ChaCha20-Poly1305 with AAD
| `openssl_kdf` | PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 (RFC 6070 case 3), HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869 case 1)
| `openssl_bignum` | `BN_mod_exp`, hex round trip, modular inverse, primality
| `openssl_random` | `RAND_status` / `RAND_bytes` / `RAND_priv_bytes`
| `openssl_encoding` | RFC 4648 base64 vectors, `OPENSSL_buf2hexstr` / `hexstr2buf`
| `openssl_rsa` | 2048-bit keygen, PKCS#1 v1.5 + PSS sign/verify (incl. tamper rejection), OAEP round trip, PEM round trip
| `openssl_ec` | P-256 keygen, ECDSA sign/verify + tamper rejection, ECDH agreement, X25519 derive, Ed25519 sign/verify
| `openssl_x509` | self-signed certificate: build, self-verify, name/SAN checks, DER + PEM round trips, `X509_STORE` verification
| `openssl_error` | the error stack: raise, format, clear
| `openssl_tls_memory` | *a full TLS 1.3 handshake* between a client and a server `SSL` over a `BIO` pair -- no sockets, no threads -- then application data both ways
|===

=== cURL (`lib/curl.cpp`)

[cols="1,3"]
|===
| `curl_version` | version matches the headers; TLS backend is OpenSSL; SSL/libz/brotli/zstd/HTTP3/IPv6/AsynchDNS features; protocol table
| `curl_easy_options` | `setopt`/`getinfo` round trips, unknown-option rejection, the option metadata table, `duphandle`, `reset`, `strerror`
| `curl_url_api` | full URL split into parts, relative-reference resolution, scheme requirement, `CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME`
| `curl_escape` | percent-encoding incl. binary input with an embedded NUL, RFC 3986 unreserved set
| `curl_slist` | insertion order, use as `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER`
| `curl_date` | the three date formats RFC 9110 requires, plus garbage rejection
| `curl_mime` | multipart body construction and `CURLOPT_MIMEPOST`
| `curl_file_transfer` | *a real transfer* over `file://`: body, `SIZE_DOWNLOAD`, effective URL, missing-file failure, protocol-allowlist rejection
| `curl_multi` | three concurrent transfers through `curl_multi_perform` / `curl_multi_poll` / `curl_multi_info_read`
| `curl_tls_loopback` | *curl over real TLS*: an in-process OpenSSL server on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port, a generated certificate as the only trust anchor (`CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB`), peer + host verification on. This is what proves the curl <-> OpenSSL pairing in the toolchain actually works end to end.
| `curl_https` | `https://example.com/` (opt-in, `--network`)
|===

== Results

.Linux, `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`
[source]
----
257 checks, 0 failures     (with --network; 251 without)
----

.Windows, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (under wine)
[source]
----
251 checks, 5 failures
----

All of libcrypto, all of libssl (including a full TLS 1.3 handshake), and every
part of curl except the loopback TLS transfer pass identically on both targets.
The five remaining failures are all in `curl_tls_loopback` and all follow from
one cause: curl cannot open a TCP connection on the Windows target (see below).

== Fixed: the miscompiled strchr that killed TLS on Windows

The suite's first run found `SSL_CTX_new()` returning `NULL` for *every* method
on `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` -- no TLS at all, neither libssl directly nor curl
over `https` -- with only an unhelpful
`error:0A080014:SSL routines:SSL_CTX_new_ex:reason(20)` on the stack.

=== Root cause

Not OpenSSL, and not OpenSSL's build configuration: a *runtime header* made
clang miscompile `strchr()` in any translation unit that also called `memchr()`.

`runtime/include/sprt/wrappers/libc/string.h` defined `memchr` as a forced-inline,
internal-linkage umbrella wrapper -- a module-local function literally named
`memchr`. But LLVM *synthesises* memchr calls on its own: at `-O2` and above it
folds `strchr(<string literal>, c)` into `memchr(<string literal>, c, len + 1)`,
and it resolves that call **by name** against whatever the module already
contains. Interprocedural constant propagation, meanwhile, is free to specialise
an internal function on the arguments of its only call site. The synthesised call
then inherits those constants and searches for the wrong byte.

Reduced to two functions -- any TU that does both is affected:

[source,c]
----
static const char prefixes[] = {'/', ':', '?', '*', '-', '\0'};
int hasZero(const void *p, size_t n) { return memchr(p, 0, n) != NULL; }
const char *findPrefix(const char *e) { return strchr(prefixes, e[0]); }
----

`findPrefix` compiled to `__sprt_memchr_impl(prefixes, 0, 6)` -- the search
character taken from the *other* function's call.

In OpenSSL this hit `gid_cb()` (`ssl/t1_lib.c`), which classifies group-list
prefix characters with `strchr(prefixes, elem[0])`:

[source]
----
Linux    movsbl (%r15),%esi     ; c = elem[0]      correct
Windows  movl   $0x2,%edx       ; c = 2            the load is gone
----

`prefixes` holds no `0x02`, so `strchr` always returned `NULL`, the `?`
(ignore-unknown) and `*` (key-share) prefixes were never consumed, and the first
entry of OpenSSL's built-in default group list -- `?*X25519MLKEM768` -- became an
unknown group that must not be ignored. `gid_cb` returned 0, so
`SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list()` failed, so `ssl_load_groups()` failed, so
`SSL_CTX_new()` aborted.

=== The fix

`memchr` is now a plain prototype instead of an umbrella inline
(`runtime/include/sprt/wrappers/libc/string.h`). It is the only umbrella wrapper
whose name LLVM emits -- its neighbours (`memcpy`, `memset`, `strchr`, ...) are
already plain declarations on the targets that route them through an import
library -- and the runtime defines the symbol itself from musl-libc, so a
prototype links exactly like any other libc call.

Verified after the change:

* the two-function reduction and the real `ssl/t1_lib.c` both emit
  `movsbl (%rbx),%edx` again;
* OpenSSL rebuilt for `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` -- `openssl_tls_memory` completes a
  TLS 1.3 handshake (`TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`) with peer verification and
  application data in both directions;
* `tests/libc` compare.sh: 78/78 identical, no regression.

=== Still to do

Every third-party library in `toolchains/targets/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` other
than OpenSSL was built before this fix and is built at `-O3`, so any of them may
carry the same miscompile. They should be rebuilt.

== Open: curl cannot connect on x86_64-pc-windows-msvc

`curl_tls_loopback` fails with `CURLE_COULDNT_CONNECT` (7) against an in-process
OpenSSL server on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port; the server side times out waiting
for a connection that never arrives. This is *not* the strchr defect and not a
runtime socket problem:

* `tests/libc socket_stream` -- bind / listen / connect / accept and stream I/O
  over loopback TCP with the same runtime sockets -- passes on the same target;
* the port is assigned and read back correctly (no byte-order fault);
* every non-transport curl test passes.

So the fault is in curl's own connect path on this target (it uses a
non-blocking connect driven by poll/select through the winsock forwarders).
Since `curl-openssl.lib` predates the strchr fix, rebuilding curl is the first
thing to try. Note the practical consequence: `stappler_network` cannot open a
connection on Windows either until this is resolved.

== Platform notes

`file://` URLs are built differently per target (`writeTempFile` in
`lib/curl.cpp`). libcurl is a Windows build there and applies DOS path rules to
a `file:` path -- it drops the leading slash when the path starts with a drive
spec and rewrites `/` as `\` -- while the runtime spells paths POSIX-style
(`/c/dir`). The URL therefore has to name the drive the way curl expects
(`file:///c:/dir/...`) for the two conventions to meet in `open()`. A Windows
libcurl also normalises that back to `file://c:/dir/...` in
`CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL`.

== Adding a library

. Add a module to `thirdparty-modules.mk` with just the link line
  (`-l:libfoo.a`); headers need no `-I`, the sysroot's `usr/include` is already
  on the global include path.
. List the module in `LOCAL_MODULES` in the `Makefile`.
. Add `lib/foo.cpp` with the test functions, declare them in `tests.h`, and
  register them in the `s_tests` table in `main.cpp`.

Prefer published test vectors over round trips: a round trip still passes when
the library is consistently wrong.
